prompt: Which kind of requirement is "a truck may not leave until SEFAZ has authorised the CT-e"?
hint: Who made that decision, and can the design choose otherwise?

choices.text: A quality attribute of the booking flow
choices.why: It says nothing about how well something is done; it states a rule the law has already fixed.

choices.text: A constraint
choices.why: Right: a decision somebody else made, here the law, which the design respects rather than chooses.

choices.text: A functional requirement of the Driver app
choices.why: No screen behaviour is being described; the rule binds the whole flow whatever any app does.

choices.text: A requirement for the architect to negotiate with SEFAZ
choices.why: The architect does not negotiate a constraint; the job is to say what it costs, to whoever owns it.

prompt: Match each statement from Carreto to the kind of requirement it is.
hint: What it does, how well, and what was decided elsewhere.

pairs.left: A driver accepts a load from the app
The price appears in under 2 seconds
A quote is not below the ANTT floor

prompt: Why does the lesson say quality attributes shape the architecture more than features do?
hint: Think of Helena's request with two different meanings of "fast".

choices.text: Features belong to product, so the architect leaves them alone
choices.why: Who owns a feature does not decide whether it reshapes the structure; the point is about structure, not ownership.

choices.text: Features change each sprint, while qualities stay fixed for years
choices.why: Qualities change too, as R1's corridor list showed; stability is not the reason given.

choices.text: One list of features fits many structures; the qualities pick between them
choices.why: Right: the same backlog sentence led to work inside Pricing or to a change across three teams, depending on the number.

choices.text: Qualities are harder to write down than features
choices.why: They are harder to put numbers on, but the lesson's argument is about what they do to the structure.

prompt: Which of these did Helena's request leave unstated, as the lesson describes it?
hint: Something a freight veteran would not think to say.

choices.text: Quoting and booking a truck in one go, as one step
choices.why: That is the first thing she said, as the functional part of the request.

choices.text: That a driver is not told later the load went to another
choices.why: Right: she assumed it, the way nobody tells a builder the house needs a roof.

choices.text: That the flow has to be fast for the shipper who waits
choices.why: She said it, as an adjective that still needed a number.

choices.text: That shippers quote and book on a single screen in one visit
choices.why: One screen was in her first sentence, and it later turned out to be a solution rather than a requirement.

prompt: Shippers ask for invoices as PDF in Spanish for one Argentine customer. Payments can add it alone, cheaply, with no timing target. By the lesson's signs, what is it?
hint: Check the three signs of architectural impact one by one.

choices.text: Payments' to handle, off the architect's list
choices.why: Right: it is cheap to change, stays inside one team and has no measure that shapes the structure.

choices.text: Architecturally significant, since a customer asked for it
choices.why: Being asked for by a customer is business value, which says how soon, not whether it is architectural.

choices.text: A constraint, because invoices are regulated documents
choices.why: The request is a format choice for one customer; nothing here was decided by a regulator.

choices.text: A quality attribute of the invoicing service
choices.why: A PDF in another language is a behaviour, not a measure of how well something is done.

prompt: In the lesson's grid, why does "price shown in under 2 s" sit outside the top-right corner?
hint: Value and impact are two different axes.

choices.text: Shippers do not care much how quickly the price appears
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: it matters a great deal to shippers, which puts it high on value.

choices.text: It was a constraint rather than a requirement
choices.why: It is a quality attribute with a number; nobody outside Carreto imposed it.

choices.text: It is met inside Pricing, with no structural change
choices.why: Right: value says how soon; it lacks architectural impact, so it stays with the team.

choices.text: Two seconds is too vague to be tested
choices.why: Two seconds is a number and testable; vagueness is the problem of "fast", not of this line.

prompt: What did Renata's first three whys change about Helena's request?
hint: From the screen to something else.

choices.text: They showed that Pricing was too slow
choices.why: The price came back straight away; Helena said that part was fine.

choices.text: It moved from the screen to the wait
choices.why: Right: what the dispatcher needs is to know a truck is coming.

choices.text: They turned the request into a constraint
choices.why: The goal they found is a business goal, more bookings, which a design is then measured against.

choices.text: They cut the scope to quoting alone
choices.why: Nothing was cut; the work was redirected to the part that loses bookings.

prompt: Renata took the last two whys to Kátia rather than Helena. What principle does the lesson draw from that?
hint: Who could answer "why 47 minutes?"

choices.text: Technical questions are kept away from the product director
choices.why: The issue is who knows the answer, not shielding anybody from technology.

choices.text: A tech lead outranks product when it comes to requirements
choices.why: Neither outranks the other; each answered the whys that were theirs to answer.

choices.text: The business knows the goal and the team knows the cause
choices.why: Right: each why goes to whoever knows the answer.

choices.text: Five whys are asked of five different people
choices.why: "Five" is not a quota, of questions or of people.

prompt: Carreto issues 42,000 quotes a month. Moving conversion from 30% to 40%, how many more bookings a month is that?
hint: Ten percentage points of the monthly quotes.

prompt: Why does the lesson advise offering Helena numbers to react to instead of asking her for a response time?
hint: Five minutes, fifteen, an hour.

choices.text: People who cannot invent a threshold judge well which of three is wrong
choices.why: Right: asked directly she would say "instant" or make a number up; reacting to consequences, she chose.

choices.text: So that the architect picks the number and she agrees
choices.why: The architect proposes candidates; the choice stays with the business, which bears the consequence.

choices.text: Because percentiles are part of a product director's training
choices.why: Nobody asked her about percentiles; they are how the architect writes her answer down.

choices.text: To keep the meeting short
choices.why: Brevity is a side effect; the reason is getting a number she actually stands behind.

prompt: For drivers, "always available" turned into a requirement for the Driver app rather than for the servers. Why?
hint: Where are drivers when they prove a delivery?

choices.text: Drivers work fewer hours than shippers
choices.why: Drivers are on the road at all hours; the opposite of fewer.

choices.text: Server availability had already reached 99.99% for them
choices.why: Booking chose 99.5% in business hours; and no server number helps a phone with no signal.

choices.text: They prove deliveries where there is no signal
choices.why: Right: the need is recording the proof with no connection, which server redundancy does not meet.

choices.text: Diego's team owns the budget for availability
choices.why: Budget ownership was not the argument; the cause was where the failure happens.

prompt: Put Renata's steps with Helena's request in the order the lesson follows.
hint: Goal before numbers, numbers before the page.
items: Ask what happens today and why it matters
Offer numbers and ask about consequences
Write each significant requirement as a scenario
Read the page back with Helena
trap: Putting numbers on "one screen" before asking what it is for would have measured the wrong thing.

prompt: What does event storming put on the wall?
hint: Written in the past tense.

choices.text: Boxes for each service and arrows for their calls
choices.why: Boxes and arrows are kept out on purpose, along with technology words.

choices.text: The backlog, ordered by business value
choices.why: The wall holds what happens in the business, not a list of features to build.

choices.text: Domain events in time order, with hot spots
choices.why: Right: things that happened, in order, and marks where people disagree or it hurts.

choices.text: Each team's estimates for the new design
choices.why: Estimating comes much later; the workshop is about understanding the flow.

prompt: In the confirmation scenario, what does the environment part do?
hint: A Saturday-night part load.

choices.text: It names the three apps being measured
choices.why: That is the artefact.

choices.text: It limits when the number applies
choices.why: Right: business hours on an ordinary weekday, so the number is not a promise for every hour of the year.

choices.text: It says who sends the request
choices.why: That is the source, the shipper.

choices.text: It holds the 15 and 60 minute thresholds
choices.why: Those belong to the response measure.

prompt: Why does the response measure carry a second threshold, 99% within 60 minutes, beside 90% within 15?
hint: Who is the shipper outside the 90%?

choices.text: Because the SEI's six-part form requires two numbers in the measure
choices.why: The form asks for a measure; the second number was a choice made for a reason.

choices.text: To give Matching a softer target to report to the business
choices.why: It is a tighter guarantee about the tail, not a softer one.

choices.text: Sílvio asked for it to control cost
choices.why: It came from Helena's answer that past an hour the dispatcher phones someone else.

choices.text: The tenth shipper is the one who phones a competitor
choices.why: Right: a 90% target says nothing about the tail, and the tail is where bookings are lost.

prompt: Which of these is written the way the lesson says a requirement should be?
hint: What has to be true, not how.

choices.text: The Driver app stores proofs in a local database and syncs them through a queue
choices.why: That is a design; putting it in the requirement takes the choice away from Diego's team.

choices.text: A proof recorded with no signal reaches Tracking within 5 min of reconnecting
choices.why: Right: a condition with a measure, and no mechanism.

choices.text: The booking flow is fast and highly available
choices.why: Adjectives with no numbers; nobody can tell whether a design meets them.

choices.text: Shippers quote and book on one screen
choices.why: "One screen" was a solution in disguise, kept off the page.

prompt: Offering each load to twenty drivers at once would meet R1 easily. Why did it not settle the design?
hint: Diego's requirement.

choices.text: The broker could not deliver twenty offers in time
choices.why: No capacity limit was raised; the conflict was with another requirement.

choices.text: It would break R2, the drivers' requirement
choices.why: Right: drivers told "taken" too many times stop opening offers, so the trade went to Helena with both numbers.

choices.text: The ANTT floor forbids offering a load more than once
choices.why: The floor limits the price, not how a load is offered.

choices.text: Kátia's team was too small to build it
choices.why: Team size is a constraint on the page, but the reason given was the drivers' experience.

prompt: Reading the page back with Helena is not about a signature; it is two people agreeing on the same ___.
hint: What R1 holds instead of adjectives.

prompt: Why do the requirements on Renata's page carry ids such as R1 and R2?
hint: Lesson 5's records.

choices.text: So decision records cite them and the link works both ways
choices.why: Right: a reader of a decision finds its cause, and whoever changes a requirement finds what rests on it.

choices.text: To rank them by priority
choices.why: R1 is not more important than R4 because of its number; the ids are labels.

choices.text: Because the SEI method numbers its scenarios
choices.why: The reason given is tracing decisions, not following a method's convention.

choices.text: So that Helena can sign each line separately
choices.why: The lesson says the meeting is not about signatures.

prompt: R1 first named twelve corridors. Why did reading it back with Helena change it to "the corridors that carry 80% of the month's loads"?
hint: February.

choices.text: Twelve corridors were too many to monitor each week
choices.why: Monitoring was not the issue; the list itself stops being true.

choices.text: To lower the target before launch
choices.why: The measure did not change; only how the corridors are chosen.

choices.text: The busy corridors change with the season
choices.why: Right: in February the grain routes overtake half the list, and her phrasing stays true when it moves.

choices.text: The ANTT publishes the list of corridors
choices.why: The corridors are Carreto's own volume data, not a regulation.

prompt: A sales director asks: "The tracking map must be real time." Which first question follows the lesson?
hint: Goal first, then consequences.

choices.text: Should positions go over WebSockets or polling?
choices.why: A technology question before the goal; he does not think in protocols.

choices.text: What latency in milliseconds do you need?
choices.why: Asking for the number directly gets "instant" or an invented figure.

choices.text: Who looks at the map, and what for?
choices.why: Right: who waits, and what a stale position costs them, lead to a number he is able to choose.

choices.text: Can we make it 99.99% available?
choices.why: That jumps to a number that sounds serious, before anybody knows what it is for.

prompt: A flow is used 10 hours a day on 30 days a month. At 99% availability measured over those hours, how many minutes of downtime are allowed a month?
hint: Hours of use, in minutes, times 1%.

prompt: Sílvio wants 99.99% availability for the booking flow "because serious companies have it". What does the lesson have the architect do?
hint: Let them choose with something in view.

choices.text: Accept it, since finance approves the budget
choices.why: Approving a budget is not the same as seeing what the number costs.

choices.text: Show what each level costs and let the business choose with the price in view
choices.why: Right: each nine adds replicas, failover and on-call, for hours nobody books.

choices.text: Refuse, as availability is the architect's decision
choices.why: The number is negotiated with the business; the architect makes its cost visible.

choices.text: Write "highly available" so both readings are covered
choices.why: An adjective cannot be tested and covers nothing.

prompt: A request reads: "Drivers must get paid faster, using Kafka." Which belong on Renata's one page? Choose all that apply.
hint: Measures and goals, no mechanisms.

choices.text: Paid within a stated number of hours of the delivery proof, for a stated share of drivers
choices.why: Yes: a measure somebody is able to check.

choices.text: Payments publishes payout events to Kafka
choices.why: No: that is a mechanism, kept off the page so the design stays open.

choices.text: Who asked, and the goal behind it
choices.why: Yes: every line names a person and a goal.

choices.text: "Faster payouts", as the requester wrote it
choices.why: No: an adjective with no number is not something a design is held to.
